posts.content:
For most of Gong's life, investors asked me the same question: what's your engagement? DAU, MAU, time in app. Ours is best in class, which I'm happy to brag about. But I always told them it was the wrong question. It's a very 1999 question, from the days when the whole game was getting people to log in to your portal. You can still spot the PMs optimizing for it: you get a notification email and have to log in to the app to see the meat of the message.

Eilon and I set out to build an autonomous AI system for revenue teams. We wanted it ambient: you get what you need in your email, on your phone, in the tool you already have open. What matters is what the AI does, not where it shows it to you. A strange thing to say in 2016. Less strange now.

Which brings me to this month's hot debate: whose chat window, whose agent, whose "place where work happens." Headless or headed? (Or is it headful? wdyt :) Nobody agrees on that either, which tells you how much the head matters.

Separating presentation from logic and data has been good design for as long as there's been software, for one reason: the interface takes many forms and it changes. The logic and data are singular. And the screens are multiplying: Slack, email, the CRM, a few AI assistants, soon voice, maybe no screen at all. 

Increasingly the user isn't even a person. It's an agent, and agents don't care whose window they're in. They care what they know when they start.

The models are the same for everyone. The context isn't. So instead of picking a side, ask three questions about any AI you're evaluating:

1. What is it reasoning over? The stage says commit; the buyer told the rep on Tuesday they're pausing. An agent reasoning over the logged version of events gives confident answers about a deal that no longer exists. Ask where its picture of the customer comes from.

2. Do you need an answer or an operation? Chat is great for "summarize the call" or "draft the follow-up." Forecasting a pipeline or running an account over a quarter isn't a question. It's an operation. It needs a shared place to live, a rhythm to run on, and a way to see whether it worked.

3. Is the intelligence yours, or wired to one surface? If your customer context only works inside one vendor's window, you've handed part of your advantage to someone else's container. Keep it portable and the interface can change as often as it likes.

The winning play is both: intelligence wherever your people and your agents work, whether that's a app, messaging, or the CRM, AND a purpose-built place for the work that needs a team, a cadence, and a scoreboard.

The interface war will have winners, and sequels. Build on what you know about your customers and you'll be fine either way.

Got a fourth question? Bring it on!

posts.content:
Silicon Valley always has a management trend du jour.

Remember holacracy? No managers, no titles, self-organizing circles. That was going to change everything.

Around 2008 every founder needed to be a "product dictator" like Steve Jobs.(*) The actual term I've heard some founders use to describe themselves in closed forums is worse. You know what I mean. But I won't repeat it here, to spare us all the hate comments :)

Then flatflexing: real leaders manage 60 directs like Jensen. Layers are for the weak.

Now it's "Cut middle management with AI."

Don't get me wrong: streamlining the org is usually a very good idea. Fewer layers, faster decisions, smaller autonomous teams. What's not to like?

But the *framing* behind this trend misses what good managers actually do. It assumes middle managers just move information around, and AI does that now.

A tech company is not an assembly line. The best managers aren't information/work routers. They are leaders. They hire. They coach. They inspire. They spot talent early and grow the next generation of leaders. They take initiative nobody asked for. Most of them got there by being the best ICs on the team (I know, I know... not always).

So cut the routers. But if you prune leaders because a spreadsheet labeled them "management layer," you're not flattening the company. You are gutting it. You just won't feel it until two years from now, when you look around for someone who can build a team, and nobody's there.

AI can move information and do serious work. It can't grow people.

Holacracy didn't last. This trend won't either. At least not in its extreme form.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
Footnote
(*) Copying one attribute/habbit of a successful person or company and expecting their results is a classic cognitive trap. Steve Jobs shipped awesome products. Steve Jobs also made people dread sharing an elevator with him. The corollary: "If people fear me, I'll ship awesome products." Obviously wrong. The attribute you copied may have nothing to do with the success. Or it works, but only in combination with a dozen other things you didn't copy.

This is a welcome development.
I was excited to read that Jack Dorsey just launched Buzz — a Slack alternative where people and AI agents share the same chat.

The agents are cool. But the more exciting part is what's missing: walls.

Buzz is *open source and self-sovereign*. Your team's conversations belong to your team, and to whatever tools and agents you decide to point at them. This is a natural response to Slack tightening terms, restricting what third-party apps can do with conversations their own customers created. Your data, their terms.

That never lasts. In the agent era, a workspace your AI can't read is a workspace that falls behind. Lock up the data and the value simply flows somewhere else. 

Buzz is early. Maybe it wins, maybe it doesn't. But something built like it will. Or maybe Slack reopens its gates and none of this matters? Either way, users win.

Water always finds its way.

P.S. Also, great name. To infinity and beyond 🚀😎

posts.content:
"Have AI update my CRM" is one of the most requested use cases we hear at Gong.

We built it. It saves time. Customers love it.

It also won't be around forever.

I'll explain.

There are two reasons for this ask.

- Reps hate data entry. It's typing opinions into a database after the real work happened. For decades, humans were the data entry layer. So the moment AI showed up, everyone asked it to do the typing. That's asking for a faster horse.

- A "hoarding" instinct. Get everything into the CRM. Every note, every field, every update. It's a relic of a CRM-centric worldview. But most of it just sits there collecting dust. Nobody reads it. Almost nothing acts on it. It's dead weight.

And CRM isn't even the best repository for this. Customer interactions are rich and unstructured. Calls, emails, messages, meetings. They capture hesitation. A competitor mentioned in passing. A champion going quiet. A budget caveat buried in an email thread.

Now reduce all that into "Loss Reason:" dropdown list.
Every CRM field is lossy compression of reality.

"AI that updates my CRM" is taking the best technology ever built for understanding rich unstructured data, and using it to throw away most of it.

One more issue: a field can only answer a question someone thought to ask in advance. Most real questions are new and ad-hoc. That's how companies end up with 600+ custom fields (a real number!). Each one a fossil of a question somebody asked once.

Where does this end up? The 600+ CRM fields become irrelevant, because the interactions themselves become the system of record. Directly queryable. Nothing lost in translation.

The CRM field update will have a good run. But it will fade away one day.

posts.content:
💰 AI PRICING is going to be hybrid. 💰 

Here's why.

- Pure per-seat doesn't work for agents.

A company with 100 users can run 100 agent tasks a day or 10 million. The headcount doesn't change. The workload does.

- Pure consumption also doesn't work.

CFOs hate it. "Your bill could be $50K or $5M depending on usage" is not a sentence that flies.

So what wins?

Think: your phone plan.

Remember when it used to be per minute and megabytes? We moved away from it.

Flat rate for the predictable stuff. Variable for the unpredictable stuff. You know exactly what your plan costs. International roaming is based on usage.

AI will land in a similar place.

Fixed fee covers the predictable stuff, including some agentic work: the AI agents and assistants that run on a reasonable cadence, bounded context, expected volume. That's budgetable.

Variable kicks in when it's not bounded. Agent runs 50,000 times a day, at random. Context window blows up on a very large query. That's when consumption pricing makes more sense.

The makers who figure out the right split win enterprise. The ones pushing pure consumption will lose deals to budget anxiety. The ones holding onto pure seats will watch their economics collapse as agents scale.

Hybrid is the model that works for both sides.

Every mature category got here eventually. AI is next. 😎

posts.content:
Would you wear Dior to the gym?

A couple of years ago, everyone asked the same question: "which model are you using?"

That's not the question today.

There are roughly three tiers now:

1. "The couture." The frontier models. For high-impact work and hard reasoning.

2. "Nordstrom Rack." Last year's designer, still a designer. Great for everyday work at a fraction of the cost.

3. "Uniqlo." The open-source models.  High-volume, low-stakes work for next to nothing. Great value.

The gap between top and bottom is often 10x or more on cost, and the lighter models usually answer faster. For simple tasks, going lighter isn't a pure compromise. You don't sprint in a ballgown.

So the choice is now made in the application layer. Sometimes a product manager makes the call, sometimes the user, increasingly the system itself, in real time.

And this part compounds. Every time you pick a model and sees how the result lands, you learns. Which model wins which task stops being a guess and becomes data. The wardrobe is the easy part. The taste is what's hard to acquire.

Soon, picking a model by hand will be out of fashion :)

posts.content:
I'm realizing that many revenue teams are measuring AI the wrong way. 

In most functions, AI has one job: do the work cheaper/faster. Legal, finance, support... you automate the task, cut the cost, done. One lever.

But in revenue, job #1 isn't just a cost to shrink. It's an outcome you can actually make more likely. So you get a second lever, and the beauty is that the two of them *multiply*. 

- Lever 1 is more selling time. Automation clears the admin work, so reps actually spend more time in front of customers. 

- Lever 2 is better craftsmanship. The AI sharpens every interaction, so more of that time converts. Higher win rates. Larger deal size. 

Think: more at-bats times a better batting average. That's way more runs :)

Here's the part most teams miss. They impelment Revenue AI and then grade it on hours saved. 
But do the math: an AE normally carries a quota that's 3 to 5x their fully loaded cost. The cost you're cutting is cool, but it's the smaller number. The revenue you're unlocking is the big one.
So if all you're counting is the time you save, you're not scoring half. You're missing the part that literally pays your salaries. 

How's your revenue team measuring AI right now? Capacity, conversion, or both?

posts.content:
How far are we from agents replacing human sellers?

Short answer: not even close. At least not in complex B2B / enterprise.

Everyone compares this to coding. That’s a mistake.

Coding has clean data, clear outcomes, tight feedback loops.
 
Sales has messy data, fuzzy truth, and most deals fail. You’re training on a system where failure is the majority outcome.

Now layer on reality.

1. Sales runs on missing information. You don’t know the real budget, the internal politics, what competitors are saying, or what happens when you’re not in the room. A lot of the truth never even makes it into the system. It happens over dinners, side conversations, hallway moments.

2. You’re not selling to a buyer. You’re navigating a buying group with conflicting incentives and power dynamics. It’s hard for humans to read. For an agent, it’s guesswork.

3. Time is the devil. Every day introduces risk. You need to push, but push too hard and you’re out. Don’t push enough and you’re also out. That balance is not something you brute-force with automation.

So no, agents aren’t replacing human sellers anytime soon.

But they will dominate parts of the job.

Anything that looks like execution and consistency, agents will crush. Prospecting, qualification, handling known objections, and especially follow-ups that never slip.

And the part humans hate most, the messy middle of the deal. Chasing stakeholders, coordinating next steps, recapping decisions, keeping momentum alive. Agents don’t get tired, don’t avoid awkward follow-ups, and don’t drop the ball.

Agents won’t replace sellers.

But sellers without agents?  Good luck! :)

posts.content:
DISCLAIMER: I run a tech company. So take this with the grain of salt if you want :)

But recent posts here reminded me, as someone who sees the "bills" every month, that many builders underestimate the cost by 5x-10x.

Not the build cost. 
The own-it-for-a-while cost. 
Building is 10%. Running and supporting is the unglamorous 90%. 

So here's a real-world checklist.
Every unchecked box is a cost, whether you build OR buy. This isn't a case for buying. It's a case for planning for the work.

PRODUCTION
[] Who's on-call at 3am?
[] What's our uptime SLA, and who signs it?
[] How do we catch bugs before users do?

SECURITY & COMPLIANCE
[] Who runs security forever, not just at launch?
[] SOC2, GDPR, HIPAA. Who owns each, and the audits?
[] Pen tests, vulnerability scans & patching, key rotation. On whose calendar?

THE STACK TAX
[] Every integration we build is one we maintain when the API breaks. Who's on it?
[] How do we evolve the data model without breaking customers?
[] Backward compatibility: today's feature is a future contract. Who holds that line?
[] Deploys, rollbacks, feature flags. Is our release pipeline managed?

PERFORMANCE & COST
[] Fast at 1K rows. Still fast at 1M?
[] Who watches the infra/token $$?
[] Who optimizes compute and storage every month/quarter?

DOCS & SUPPORT
[] User docs and internal docs. Who owns them in year 3?
[] When tickets come in, who answers?
[] Is helpdesk a side hustle or a real function?

PEOPLE
[] Can we hire and retain engineers as good as a vendor whose only job is this?
[] If developers leave, who takes over?
[] Is the knowledge written down, or in someone's head?

Sometimes building is right. When it's your edge, build it and own every box on this list with pride. When it's not, buy it.

Feel free to modify this checklist. It's yours 😎

posts.content:
If you are feeding AI only call transcripts, you are doing it wrong.

Gong Labs ran a study across 821 AI field evaluations to answer a simple question:

IF you remove email… how WRONG do you get?❓ 🤔 

Pretty wrong.

• Emails added meaningful, non-redundant signal in 85.4% of cases
 • Calls alone were sufficient only 35.6% of the time
 • Similarity to the full picture, calls only: 3.4 / 5
 • Similarity to the full picture, emails only: 3.0 / 5

In other words:

If you’re only using calls, you’re missing the real picture most of the time.
And here’s where it shows up with near certainty:

Next steps
- 100% email value
- 0–4% calls-sufficient
 This is where decisions actually get finalized.

Why deals are lost
- 100% email value
- 6–14% calls-sufficient
 The real reasons show up after the call.

Deal stage
- Up to 100% email value
 Contracts, POs, scheduling… all email.

Even basic CRM fields
 → 79% email value
 → Email changes the answer ~35% of the time.

Calls tell you what people say in the moment.
Emails tell you what people do.

If your AI, forecasting, or pipeline reviews don’t include email, you’re not seeing the deal.
You’re looking at it through a peephole. 🙈
